amino-acid.definition: A small molecule that is a building block of peptides and proteins. There are 20 standard kinds; each has an amino end, an acid end and its own side chain.

peptide.definition: A short chain of amino acids, typically 2 to about 50, joined by peptide bonds. Many hormones and some medicines are peptides.

polypeptide.definition: A longer chain of amino acids. One or more polypeptides fold together to make a protein.

protein.definition: A long chain of amino acids, or several chains, folded into a fixed shape. Where a peptide ends and a protein begins is a convention, not a natural line.

peptide-bond.definition: The chemical link between two amino acids in a chain. Digestive and other enzymes break it by adding water (hydrolysis).

condensation-reaction.definition: A chemical reaction that joins two molecules and gives off a small molecule, usually water. Joining amino acids into a chain is a condensation.

hydrolysis.definition: Breaking a chemical bond by adding water. Digestion breaks protein and peptides this way.

n-terminus.definition: The start of a peptide chain, where a free amino group sits unless it has been changed. Sequences are written from here.

c-terminus.definition: The end of a peptide chain, where a free acid group sits unless it has been changed.

primary-structure.definition: The order of the amino acids in a peptide or protein chain: its sequence.

secondary-structure.definition: Local twists or pleats in a peptide chain, such as a spiral (helix) or a flat sheet, held mainly by hydrogen bonds.

tertiary-structure.definition: The overall three-dimensional fold of a whole chain, held by contacts between its side chains and sometimes by sulfur bridges.

quaternary-structure.definition: Two or more chains fitted together into one working unit.

hydrogen-bond.definition: A weak attraction between a hydrogen atom and a nearby oxygen or nitrogen atom. Many of them together hold a peptide chain in a twist or fold.

disulfide-bond.definition: A strong link between two sulfur atoms, usually from two cysteine amino acids. It can close a chain into a ring or tie two chains together.

dalton.definition: The unit for the mass of a molecule. One dalton is roughly the mass of one hydrogen atom.

d-amino-acid.definition: The mirror-image form of an amino acid. The body builds its proteins from the other form (L); enzymes that fit L-chains often cannot cut at a D-amino acid.

racemisation.definition: An amino acid flipping into its mirror-image form during manufacture. It creates an impurity that looks almost the same as the wanted peptide.

cyclic-peptide.definition: A peptide whose chain is closed into a ring. Rings have no loose ends for some enzymes and a more rigid shape, so they often last longer.

pegylation.definition: Attaching chains of polyethylene glycol (PEG) to a medicine. It makes the molecule bigger, so the kidneys filter it less, and shields it from enzymes.

fc-fusion.definition: Joining a medicine to a piece of an antibody (the Fc part). The bigger molecule is filtered less by the kidneys and lasts longer.

solid-phase-peptide-synthesis.definition: The usual chemical way to make peptides: the chain is built on tiny resin beads, one amino acid at a time, with washing between steps.

protecting-group.definition: A temporary chemical cap that stops part of an amino acid reacting at the wrong moment during synthesis. It is removed later.

receptor.definition: A protein on or in a cell that a hormone or medicine fits into, like a key in a lock. When it is switched on, the cell responds.

g-protein-coupled-receptor.definition: A large family of receptors that sit in the cell's outer wall and pass a signal inside through a G protein. Many peptide hormones act on them.

g-protein.definition: A switch protein just inside the cell wall. A switched-on receptor activates it, and it passes the signal to an enzyme.

second-messenger.definition: A small molecule made inside a cell when a receptor on the surface is switched on. It carries the message further into the cell. cAMP is one.

adenylate-cyclase.definition: The enzyme that makes the messenger cAMP inside a cell when a G protein switches it on.

kinase.definition: An enzyme that switches other proteins on or off by attaching a phosphate group to them. PKA is a kinase that cAMP switches on.

affinity.definition: How tightly a molecule grips its receptor. High affinity does not by itself mean a strong effect.

intrinsic-efficacy.definition: How strongly a molecule switches a receptor on once it is bound. Agonists have it; antagonists do not.

potency.definition: How much of a drug is needed for a given effect. A potent drug works at a small amount.

full-agonist.definition: A molecule that switches a receptor on as fully as the cell allows.

partial-agonist.definition: A molecule that switches a receptor on only part of the way, even when it fills every receptor. It can weaken the effect of a stronger agonist.

antagonist.definition: A molecule that binds a receptor without switching it on, so it blocks the body's own signal.

inverse-agonist.definition: A molecule that turns down a receptor that is active on its own, the opposite of an agonist.

selectivity.definition: A drug's preference for one target over others. It is never absolute: at higher amounts a drug acts on more targets.

off-target-effect.definition: An effect caused by a drug acting on something other than its intended target.

drug-tolerance.definition: A weaker response to a drug after repeated or long use, for example because cells have fewer working receptors.

negative-feedback.definition: A control loop in which a result slows its own source, like a thermostat. Many hormone systems are controlled this way.

hypothalamus.definition: A small area at the base of the brain that controls many hormones, mostly by giving orders to the pituitary gland.

pituitary-gland.definition: A pea-sized gland under the brain that releases hormones, such as growth hormone, LH and FSH, which control other glands.

growth-hormone.definition: A hormone from the pituitary gland that drives growth and affects metabolism, partly by raising IGF-1. It is released in pulses.

somatostatin.definition: A natural peptide hormone that acts as a brake on the release of growth hormone and other hormones. It lasts only minutes in the blood.

gnrh.definition: A peptide hormone from the brain, released in pulses, that tells the pituitary to release LH and FSH, which keep the sex hormones going.

lh-and-fsh.definition: Two hormones from the pituitary gland that make the testes and ovaries produce sex hormones and sperm or eggs.

castrate-level.definition: A testosterone level as low as after removal of the testes. Some prostate cancer treatments aim for it on purpose.

melanocyte.definition: A skin cell that makes the dark pigment melanin.

pharmacokinetics.definition: What the body does to a medicine: how it is absorbed, spread, broken down and removed, and how fast.

adme.definition: Short for absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion: the four things the body does to a medicine.

bioavailability.definition: The share of a dose that reaches the bloodstream unchanged, compared with an injection straight into a vein.

clearance.definition: How quickly the body removes a medicine, measured as the volume of plasma (the liquid part of the blood) cleared of it per unit of time, for example per hour.

volume-of-distribution.definition: A measure of how far a medicine spreads from the blood into the tissues. It is a calculated number, not a real space in the body.

steady-state.definition: The level a medicine settles at with regular use, when the amount removed between doses equals the amount given. It takes about four to five half-lives to get close.

first-pass-metabolism.definition: Breakdown of a swallowed medicine in the gut wall or liver before it reaches the rest of the body.

protease.definition: An enzyme that cuts the bonds between amino acids. Proteases work in the gut, the blood and most tissues.

neutral-endopeptidase.definition: An enzyme that cuts peptides. It is one of the enzymes that break down semaglutide.

glomerulus.definition: The tiny filter in the kidney that strains waste out of the blood. It lets small molecules, including most peptides, through and holds back large proteins such as albumin.

lymph.definition: Clear fluid that drains from tissues through its own vessels back into the blood. Large molecules injected under the skin travel partly this way.

intravenous.definition: Given straight into a vein. The whole dose reaches the blood at once.

pepsin.definition: The main protein-cutting enzyme of the stomach. It works in strong acid and stops working when the acid is neutralised.

trypsin.definition: One of several protein-cutting enzymes that the pancreas releases into the small intestine to digest food protein.

brush-border.definition: The surface of the cells lining the small intestine, covered with tiny projections and enzymes that finish digesting protein into amino acids.

tight-junction.definition: A seal between neighbouring cells of a lining, such as the gut wall. It keeps large molecules from slipping between the cells.

hydrophilic.definition: Attracted to water. Water-loving molecules dissolve well in blood but pass poorly through the oily walls of cells.

cell-membrane.definition: The thin, oily outer wall of a cell. Small, fat-loving molecules pass through it; large, water-loving ones mostly do not.

small-molecule.definition: A medicine made of a small chemical rather than a chain of amino acids. Most pills are small molecules.

rule-of-five.definition: A rule of thumb from drug chemistry: a swallowed drug is less likely to be absorbed well if, among other things, it weighs more than 500 daltons.

permeation-enhancer.definition: An added substance that helps a medicine pass through a lining, such as the gut wall. SNAC in semaglutide tablets is one.

sublingual.definition: Taken by letting it dissolve under the tongue, so that it is absorbed through the lining of the mouth.

intranasal.definition: Given into the nose, as a spray or drops, to be absorbed through the lining of the nose.

cyp3a4.definition: A liver enzyme that breaks down many medicines. Other drugs that block or speed it up can change how much of a medicine stays in the body.

boxed-warning.definition: The strongest warning on a US medicine label, printed in a box at the top.
